History and Physical (H&P – Super Detailed)

Consult Summary:
26-year-old woman with 3-day history of new, red, dry, intensely itchy rash on arms and hands that began after swimming; no systemic symptoms; likely contact/irritant dermatitis, plan for topical steroid, emollient, oral antihistamine, and follow-up.

History:
• Presenting complaint – diffuse dry, itchy, red skin on forearms and hands.  
• Onset/progression – began “a few days ago,” first noticed after a swimming session; persistent since onset, not improving with self-applied coconut butter.  
• Location – bilateral arms and hands; no spread to chest, legs, or face.  
• Character – pruritus, erythema, dryness; denies pain, cracking, discharge, bleeding, pustules, or spots.  
• Associated symptoms – no fever, night sweats, vomiting, diarrhea, or systemic illness; reports feeling “quite tired” but maintaining normal appetite, hydration, bowel and bladder function.  
• Exacerbating/relieving factors – possible trigger: exposure to chlorinated pool water; stress at work; coconut butter ineffective; has not tried other therapies yet.  
• Review of systems – negative for respiratory, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, genitourinary, neurological complaints.  
 
Past Medical History:
• No chronic medical conditions reported.  
• No previous eczema, dermatitis, or other dermatologic conditions.  
• Self-reported lactose intolerance (food intolerance; not confirmed).  
• Medications – Microgynon (combined oral contraceptive pill, dose/route/frequency not documented).  
• No other regular medications.  
 
Allergies:
• Drug allergies: none reported.  
• Food intolerance: possible lactose intolerance (patient-reported).  
 
Social History:
• Occupation – primary school teacher; currently under increased work stress and long hours.  
• Living situation – lives alone.  
• Tobacco – non-smoker.  
• Alcohol – denies significant use.  
• Recreational drugs – denies.  
• Recent activities – swimming several days ago (first episode preceding rash; has swum previously without problems).  
 
Family History:
• Father – asthma.  
• Mother – hay fever.  
• No known family history of dermatologic disease.  
 
Physical Examination:
(No in-person examination performed; teleconsult.)  
Patient-reported findings: diffuse erythematous, dry, pruritic rash on bilateral arms and hands; no cracking, oozing, or bleeding; afebrile per history; appears otherwise well.  
 
Investigations:
• None obtained during this visit.  
 
Assessment & Plan:

Issue 1 – Acute pruritic dermatitis of arms/hands  
• Assessment: Likely irritant contact dermatitis from recent chlorinated pool exposure; differentials include atopic dermatitis flare and allergic contact dermatitis. No features of infection or systemic involvement.  
• Plan:  
  – Initiate moderate-potency topical corticosteroid cream (e.g., hydrocortisone 1% or equivalent; specific product/dose not documented).  
  – Regular liberal use of bland emollients throughout the day.  
  – Oral non-sedating antihistamine (e.g., loratadine) or sedating antihistamine (chlorphenamine/Piriton) for itch; OTC per patient preference.  
  – Patient information leaflet on dermatitis and skin care.  
  – Avoid/reduce exposure to potential irritants (chlorinated pools, harsh soaps/detergents).  
  – Reassess in 1 week if no improvement or sooner if worsening (arrange follow-up appointment).

Issue 2 – Work-related stress and fatigue  
• Assessment: Increased occupational stress may exacerbate skin symptoms and contribute to tiredness.  
• Plan:  
  – Advise stress-reduction strategies (breaks, sleep hygiene, workload management).  
  – Encourage return visit if ongoing fatigue or mood concerns develop.

General advice  
• No role for systemic analgesics at present; paracetamol not required as pain absent.  
• Emergency advice: seek care if rash spreads rapidly, develops pain, swelling, discharge, fever, or if systemic symptoms occur.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Irritant contact dermatitis (chlorine exposure) – High likelihood; acute onset after swimming, distribution limited to exposed areas, typical dryness and erythema, absence of vesicles or systemic signs.  
2. Atopic dermatitis (eczema) – Moderate likelihood; pruritus, dry skin, family atopy, stress trigger, but no past personal history and clear exposure history make this secondary.  
3. Allergic contact dermatitis – Moderate likelihood; immune-mediated reaction to chlorine or other contactant fits chronology; lack of vesiculation or prior pool reaction slightly lowers probability.

Quality checks:

● Missing but clinically expected elements: vital signs, full drug/allergy reconciliation, exact steroid/antihistamine dosage instructions, documentation of skin exam findings (morphology, distribution) by clinician, vaccination status.  
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx: none significant; DDx supportive of clinician’s impression.  
● Transcript quality: clear, minor inaudible segments but key clinical information intact.
